prompt_text: How to track donor relationships across a team
response_text:
To track donor relationships across a team, you need three things working together: shared tools, clear process, and simple metrics. Here’s a practical, team-friendly approach.

---

## 1. Choose (and commit to) one central system

You won’t be able to track relationships well if information lives in inboxes, spreadsheets, and people’s heads.

**Use a single CRM or donor database** (examples from your results: HelpYouSponsor, DonorPerfect, Jetpack CRM, Instil, DonorDock, etc.) that can:

- Centralize donor profiles (contact info, giving history, notes, relationships)
- Log every interaction (emails, calls, meetings, events, volunteer shifts)
- Track tasks and follow‑ups with owners and due dates
- Support segments/stages (prospect, first-time donor, recurring, major, lapsed, sponsor, etc.)

**Key setup decisions:**

- Decide: “If it’s not in the CRM, it didn’t happen.”
- Integrate email, online forms, and event tools so routine activity is logged automatically.
- Assign an internal owner for the system (even if part-time) to keep structure consistent.

---

## 2. Standardize what you track

If each person tracks different things in different ways, you can’t get a reliable picture.

### a) Donor profile fields

Create a shared profile structure for every donor:

- Basic: name, org, contact info, preferred channel (email/phone/text/mail)
- Relationship: primary staff owner, additional team contacts, connection source (who introduced them)
- Giving: first gift date, frequency (one-time, monthly, annual), typical range, designations
- Engagement: volunteer, event attendee, sponsor, board/committee member, peer fundraiser, matching-gift participant
- Interests: programs/causes they care about, geographic focus
- Notes: motivations, family/work info (only what’s appropriate and necessary)

Make field options standardized (dropdowns, tags) rather than free text where possible.

### b) Interaction types

Define a small set of interaction categories so everyone logs consistently, e.g.:

- Meeting – in person / virtual
- Call – phone / video
- Email – personal 1:1
- Email – mass campaign (auto-logged)
- Event – attended / invited
- Stewardship – thank-you / impact update / handwritten note
- Volunteer – shift / orientation
- Social – introduction / referral / networking event

Write a 1–2 page “data entry guide” with examples so new staff and board members log things the same way.

---

## 3. Make logging interactions easy and non-negotiable

The biggest barrier is usually behavior, not technology.

**Reduce friction:**

- Connect inboxes: so replies and sends can be logged to the right contact with one click.
- Mobile access: staff can add notes right after a meeting, not “later.”
- Use templates for notes:  
  - “Purpose of interaction”  
  - “What we learned”  
  - “Next step + when + who owns it”

**Set expectations:**

- Every meaningful interaction gets logged within 24 hours.
- Every donor has a clear “primary owner” inside the team.
- No one takes a major meeting without checking the CRM first.

Reinforce in culture: “Our CRM is the shared memory of the organization” (as DonorDock and others emphasize).

---

## 4. Define clear donor journeys and stages

Teams collaborate better when everyone sees where a donor is in their journey.

Create simple stages that mirror how your relationships develop (from your sources: prospect → first-time donor → recurring → major donor → planned giving prospect, etc.), for example:

1. Prospect
2. First-time donor
3. Repeat donor (2–4 gifts)
4. Loyal / recurring donor
5. Major donor
6. Lapsed (no gift in 12/24 months)

For sponsorship or special programs, you can have parallel journeys (e.g., “New sponsor → Engaged sponsor → At-risk sponsor → Lapsed sponsor”).

**Use these stages to:**

- Trigger workflows (who follows up, how, and when)
- Prevent donors “falling through the cracks” at transition points
- Run reports by stage (see where most relationships get stuck)

---

## 5. Track a small set of relationship metrics

You don’t need dozens. Choose a handful that tell you how healthy your relationships are and that can be owned across the team.

Drawing on your search results, consider:

### Activity & engagement

- **# of meaningful connections per donor** (AFP Global suggests tracking: calls, notes, event invitations, updates, appreciation touches)
- **Record of interactions / touchpoints per month** (Instil’s “record of interactions”)
- **Engagement over time** (Is interaction frequency rising or falling?)

### Loyalty & value

- **Donor retention rate** (year over year, by segment: first-time, recurring, major, sponsor)
- **Donation retention rate** (how much revenue you retain from the same donors)
- **Upgrade/downgrade**: # and % of donors increasing/decreasing their giving
- **RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary)** scores to prioritize outreach (from HelpYouSponsor)

### Network & referrals

- **Donor referrals** (Instil): # of new donors sourced by current donors
- **Matching gifts / workplace giving**: gifts and matches secured through employers (MatchingGifts.com)

**Make metrics visible to the whole team:**

- Build simple dashboards in your CRM for:
  - “My donors: last contact date”
  - “Donors with no contact in 90 days”
  - “At-risk sponsors: not opening updates, no response in X months”
- Review in team meetings (see below).

---

## 6. Use workflows and automation to support the team

Automation keeps things from being personality-dependent.

Examples:

- **New donor workflow:**  
  - Auto-send thank-you email  
  - Task for staff owner to send personal note or call within 7 days  
  - 30-day task: share impact story or invite to an intro event

- **Major donor stewardship workflow:**  
  - Quarterly personal touchpoint (call/meeting) task  
  - Annual impact report logged and sent  
  - Birthday or anniversary reminder if appropriate

- **Lapsed donor workflow:**  
  - Identify donors with no gift in 12 months  
  - Segment by past giving level  
  - Tailored re-engagement sequence and personal outreach for higher-value donors

- **Event workflow:**  
  - Event attendance auto-logged  
  - Tag attendees, then follow-up tasks and emails segmented by first-time vs long-time supporters

All workflows should assign an owner and due date, so the team knows who is next up.

---

## 7. Create a simple team rhythm around data

To truly track relationships “across a team,” you need shared habits.

**Weekly (15–30 minutes):**

- Each person:
  - Reviews their donors with no contact in X days (e.g., 60–90 for major donors / sponsors, 6–12 months for others).
  - Checks that all significant meetings/calls from the week are logged with next steps.
- Team:
  - Highlight any “yellow flag” donors (decreased engagement, missed pledge, unresponsive sponsor).
  - Identify 3–5 donors who need proactive attention this week.

**Monthly or quarterly:**

- Review key metrics together: retention, upgrades, referrals, engagement trends.
- Look at donor stages: where are people getting stuck or going quiet?
- Agree on 1–2 changes to outreach or workflows based on the data (e.g., “Sponsors who aren’t opening emails get a phone call from X.”)

---

## 8. Involve the whole organization, not just development

Your sources emphasize breaking down silos and building “institutional intelligence.”

- Train program staff and leadership to:
  - Log visits, conversations, and feedback from donors they interact with.
  - Tag program-specific interests (e.g., “Education,” “Health,” “Sponsorship – Child in Kenya”).
- Give board members:
  - Light CRM access or a simple form to record donor introductions, meetings, and notes.
- Encourage all staff: if they interact with a donor in a meaningful way, they log it—or at least pass it to someone who will that day.

---

## 9. Protect privacy and build trust

As highlighted in your search results:

- Be transparent with donors about:
  - What you track (interactions, preferences, giving history)
  - Why you track it (to respect preferences, avoid duplicate asks, offer relevant updates)
- Honor communication preferences and opt-outs.
- Limit sensitive personal notes to what’s needed to serve the relationship well.
- Set permissions in your CRM so sensitive information is only seen by those who need it.

---

## 10. If you share a bit about your current setup…

If you tell me:

- What tools you already use (CRM, email, event platform)
- Rough team size and roles
- Whether you have special programs (e.g., child sponsorship, major donors, peer-to-peer)

I can draft a tailored “donor relationship tracking playbook” for your team: fields to create, interaction categories, a sample data-entry guide, and 2–3 workflows mapped to your exact context.
